title: What is the difference between the JDK, the JRE, and the JVM, and who needs which one?
shortTitle: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime engine that loads bytecode, verifies it, manages memory, and executes it on a specific operating system. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard class libraries and supporting files needed to RUN a Java application. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools such as the compiler `javac`, the debugger, `jar`, and `javadoc`, needed to BUILD Java applications.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to run a money-transfer application. The JVM is like the actual cash-counting machine that physically processes each note. The JRE is that machine plus the standard forms, rubber stamps, and rule books the clerk needs to serve customers. The JDK is everything the JRE has PLUS the full workshop with tools where engineers like Rajesh actually design and build new banking features. A customer-facing branch only needs the machine and forms (JRE) to serve Priya. But Rajesh, the developer, needs the full workshop (JDK) to create the transfer feature in the first place.
s1_definition.oneliner: JDK builds it, JRE runs it, JVM executes it — JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime engine that loads bytecode, verifies it, manages memory, and executes it on a specific operating system. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard class libraries and supporting files needed to RUN a Java application. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus development tools such as the compiler `javac`, the debugger, `jar`, and `javadoc`, needed to BUILD Java applications.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants to run a money-transfer application. The JVM is like the actual cash-counting machine that physically processes each note. The JRE is that machine plus the standard forms, rubber stamps, and rule books the clerk needs to serve customers. The JDK is everything the JRE has PLUS the full workshop with tools where engineers like Rajesh actually design and build new banking features. A customer-facing branch only needs the machine and forms (JRE) to serve Priya. But Rajesh, the developer, needs the full workshop (JDK) to create the transfer feature in the first place.

**One line to remember:** JDK builds it, JRE runs it, JVM executes it — JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM.

sections.s2_technical:
The JVM is an abstract computing machine defined by a specification. Its job is to take platform-neutral bytecode (the `.class` files produced by the compiler) and turn it into real machine instructions for the CPU it is running on. The JVM is responsible for class loading, bytecode verification, memory management through the heap and stacks, garbage collection, and Just-In-Time compilation of frequently executed code into native machine code for speed.

The JRE wraps the JVM together with everything an application needs at runtime. This includes the core libraries such as `java.lang`, `java.util`, and `java.math`. For banking, `java.math.BigDecimal` lives in the JRE libraries. When you write `BigDecimal balance = new BigDecimal("1000000.00")`, the class definition for `BigDecimal` is provided by the JRE. The JRE alone cannot compile source code — it can only run already-compiled bytecode.

The JDK is a superset of the JRE. It adds the tools developers need. The most important is `javac`, the compiler that turns `Account.java` into `Account.class`. It also includes `jar` for packaging, `javadoc` for documentation, `jdb` for debugging, `jshell` for interactive experiments, and `javap` for inspecting bytecode. A senior nuance is that from Java 11 onward, Oracle stopped shipping a separate standalone public JRE; instead you create a trimmed runtime image using `jlink` from the modular JDK. So in modern deployments, you often ship a custom runtime image rather than a classic JRE.

A second senior nuance is the difference between the JVM specification and a JVM implementation. HotSpot (from Oracle and OpenJDK) and OpenJ9 (from Eclipse) are both implementations of the same specification. They differ in their garbage collectors and JIT compilers, but both run the same bytecode. This is why your compiled banking jar runs identically whether the bank's servers use HotSpot or OpenJ9.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh the developer writes a small program that transfers money from his savings account to Priya's current account. Before anyone can run this, someone has to turn Rajesh's human-readable source code into something a machine can execute. This is exactly what the JDK's `javac` compiler does — it takes `TransferDemo.java` and produces `TransferDemo.class`, which contains bytecode.

Problem 2 — The branch server that actually runs the transfer every night does not need the compiler. It only needs to execute the already-built program. This is exactly what the JRE and the JVM provide — the `java` launcher starts the JVM, the JVM loads the `.class` file, verifies it, and runs it using library classes like `BigDecimal` that the JRE supplies.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to confirm which exact runtime is executing in production, because the operations team must know whether they are on HotSpot or OpenJ9 for tuning garbage collection. This is exactly what querying JVM system properties does at runtime — the program can report the vendor and version of the JVM it is running inside.

The code will have an `Account` class with `accountId`, `holderName`, `balance`, and `debit`/`credit` methods, a `TransferService` that performs the transfer, and a `TransferDemo` main class that also prints the JVM, JRE, and JDK details it is running under.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jdk-jre-jvm-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/core/
│       └── TransferDemo.java        (main + Account + TransferService)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile with the JDK's javac (only the JDK has this tool)
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/TransferDemo.java

# Run with the JRE/JVM launcher (the java command starts the JVM)
java -cp out com.bank.core.TransferDemo

# Inspect the generated bytecode (JDK tool, proves .class is bytecode)
javap -c -cp out com.bank.core.Account
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's `TransferDemo.java` source file, and a transfer of 50000 rupees from SAV2001 to CUR3001.

Step 1: Rajesh runs `javac`, which is a JDK tool. The compiler reads the human-readable `.java` source and produces `TransferDemo.class`, `Account.class`, and the others. These contain bytecode, not native machine code. At this point the data is on disk as class files.

Step 2: The operations team runs `java com.bank.core.TransferDemo`. The `java` launcher starts the JVM. The JVM is part of the JRE. No compiler is involved anymore.

Step 3: The JVM's class loader finds `TransferDemo.class` on the classpath and loads it into memory. It also loads library classes like `BigDecimal` from the JRE's own class library.

Step 4: The bytecode verifier checks the loaded bytecode is safe and well-formed before any code runs.

Step 5: Execution begins at `main`. The JVM reads system properties and reports the vendor and version — this proves which implementation is running. Then the transfer logic runs, SAV2001 is debited 50000 and CUR3001 is credited 50000.

Step 6: The final balances are computed using `BigDecimal` arithmetic from the JRE library and logged.

```text
INFO: JVM name   : OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM
INFO: JVM vendor : Eclipse Adoptium
INFO: JVM version: 17.0.9+9
INFO: Java (JRE) : 17.0.9
INFO: Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
INFO: SAV2001 new balance: 950000.00
INFO: CUR3001 new balance: 300000.00
```

```text
  Rajesh writes: TransferDemo.java  (human-readable source)
    │
    │  javac  (JDK ONLY tool)
    ▼
  TransferDemo.class + Account.class ...  (bytecode on disk)
    │
    │  java launcher  (JRE/JVM)

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              JVM                       │
  │  ClassLoader → loads .class + library │
  │       │                                │
  │       ▼                                │
  │  Bytecode Verifier → safety check     │
  │       │                                │
  │       ▼                                │
  │  Interpreter + JIT → native execution │
  └──────────────┬─────────────────────────┘

  Transfer executes: SAV2001 1,000,000 → 950,000
                     CUR3001   250,000 → 300,000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Containment Relationship JDK ⊇ JRE ⊇ JVM ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   JDK                           │
  │  + javac (compiler)                             │
  │  + jar, javadoc, jdb, jshell, javap, jlink      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                 JRE                      │   │
  │  │  + core libraries (java.lang, java.util, │   │
  │  │    java.math.BigDecimal, java.time ...)  │   │
  │  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │              JVM                  │  │   │
  │  │  │  - ClassLoader subsystem          │  │   │
  │  │  │  - Bytecode Verifier              │  │   │
  │  │  │  - Runtime Data Areas (heap,stack)│  │   │
  │  │  │  - Execution Engine (interp + JIT)│  │   │
  │  │  │  - Garbage Collector              │  │   │
  │  │  └───────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Design note (SOLID — Single Responsibility):
   JVM     : execute bytecode only
   JRE libs: provide reusable classes only
   JDK tool: build/package/debug only
   Each layer has ONE clear job.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM, the JRE, and the JDK are three nested layers of the Java platform, each with a distinct responsibility. The JVM, the Java Virtual Machine, is the runtime engine. Its job is to load compiled bytecode, verify that it is safe, manage memory through the heap and the stacks, run garbage collection, and use a Just-In-Time compiler to turn frequently executed bytecode into native machine code. The JVM is defined by a specification, and there are several implementations such as HotSpot and OpenJ9 that all run the same bytecode.

The JRE, the Java Runtime Environment, is the JVM plus the standard class libraries and supporting files that a program needs at runtime. When my banking code uses BigDecimal for money, that class comes from the JRE libraries. A machine with only the JRE can run a Java application but cannot compile source code.

The JDK, the Java Development Kit, is the JRE plus the development tools. The most important is the compiler, javac, which turns my source files into bytecode. It also includes the packager jar, the documentation tool, the debugger, and the interactive shell. The relationship is strictly nested: the JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM.

In my work at the bank, this distinction matters for deployment. Our developers and build servers need the full JDK because they compile and package the transfer service into a jar. But our production branch servers only need a runtime, so from Java 11 onward we use jlink to create a slim custom runtime image that contains just the JVM and the libraries our app actually uses. This keeps the production footprint small and the attack surface minimal.

So in one sentence, the JDK builds it, the JRE runs it, and the JVM executes it, and every developer should know that the thing making Java portable is the bytecode plus the JVM, not any single layer alone.

---

keyPoints: JVM — runtime engine that executes bytecode (class loading, GC, JIT)
JRE — JVM + standard class libraries (java.lang, java.util, java.math)
JDK — JRE + development tools (javac, jar, javadoc, jdb, jlink)
From Java 11+, no standalone JRE — use jlink for custom runtime image
HotSpot and OpenJ9 are different implementations of the same JVM spec
